sources.news_title: New York Governor Names Special Prosecutor in Cornell Sexual Assault Case
sources.text:
Rabia Iclal Turan
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
New York Governor Kathy Hochul on Friday appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor in a Cornell University sexual assault case.
A woman reported in 2024 that she was gang-raped at a Cornell fraternity house and accused campus police and local prosecutors of failing her.
“This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then, at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her,” Hochul told a news conference alongside James.
Citing new reports, Hochul said the woman told Cornell police she was “100% confident that she had been raped,” but “those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors.”
She said prosecutors declined to pursue charges after reviewing “that incomplete account” and without interviewing the woman.
“That is why I’m invoking the power conferred to me as the governor of the state of New York to enlist Attorney General James as an independent special prosecutor in this case,” Hochul said.
“And if the evidence supports criminal charges, she will pursue them,” she added.
James said her office would review the facts, gather evidence and interview witnesses, pursuing prosecutions if warranted.

sources.news_title: NY Gov. Hochul Says Cornell 7 Accuser Was Failed at Every Turn
sources.text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday that a Cornell University student who allegedly was raped by fraternity members had been “failed at every turn.” She removed the local district attorney from the case and placed state Attorney General Letitia James in charge of the investigation.
Hochul expressed outrage after learning that the accuser told investigators from the outset that she was “100%” certain she had been raped. Yet, she said, those words were “shockingly” omitted from the police report sent to prosecutors, who later declined to pursue the case.
“This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” Hochul told reporters at a Manhattan news conference Friday. “And then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
Hochul issued an executive order this week directing James to assume control of the criminal investigation. The move followed reports about the disturbing allegations, which drew national attention and prompted questions about how Cornell and local officials handled the case.
The governor said she no longer had confidence in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s investigation after new reporting uncovered discrepancies between the DA’s account of the student’s initial report and what she told Cornell police.

Van Houten said he chose not to prosecute the case in 2024 because the student’s sworn statement to Cornell University police, although disturbing, did not explicitly accuse the male students of rape.
However, a transcript of the student’s conversation with Cornell campus police and Title IX officials, obtained this week, showed that she said: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
“Yet shockingly, those words never made it into the account that Cornell police sent to prosecutors,” Hochul said.

sources.news_title: ‘Deeply disturbed’ Hochul rages at how ‘brave’ Cornell 7 accuser was ‘failed at every turn’
sources.text:
‘Deeply disturbed’ Hochul rages at how ‘brave’ ‘Cornell 7’ accuser was ‘failed at every turn’ in ‘utterly unspeakable’ ordeal
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul raged Friday that the Cornell University student who was allegedly gang raped by fraternity members was “failed at every turn” — as she kicked the local district attorney off the case and put state Attorney General Letitia James in charge of the investigation.
Hochul could not hide her anger at learning the accuser told investigators from the off that she was “100%” confident she’d been raped — but “shockingly” those words never made it into the police report sent to prosecutors, who then dropped the case.
“In what world would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?” Hochul asked at a press conference in Manhattan on Friday.
“In what world does the district not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request a full transcript?” she asked with visible contempt.
“This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
Hochul directed James to take over the criminal investigation by executive order this week after news of the stomach-churning rape allegations shook the nation and raised questions about how school and local officials handled the case.
James declared the Cornell case an “active criminal investigation.”
“We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and if warranted pursue prosecutions,” James said. “I know that you want answers. I do, too.”
The governor said she lost confidence in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s investigation after new reporting revealed discrepancies in what the DA said the survivor originally reported to campus police.
Van Houten said he decided against prosecuting the case in 2024 because the student’s sworn statement to Cornell University police, while disturbing, did not accuse the male students of rape.
However, a transcript of Doe’s conversation with Cornell campus police and Title IX revealed this week that she had told them. “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
“Yet shockingly. Those words never made it into the account; those words never made it to the account that the Cornell police set to prosecutors,” Hochul said.
Van Houten has claimed he never received the full transcript, only a six-page summary statement from police.
The new revelations raise “serious questions about the information [Van Houten’s] office relied upon when it made that decision,” Hochul added.
The governor didn’t hold back punches in blasting the Cornell police department for not supplying all its evidence to the DA’s office, and for the DA deciding not to interview the victim, anyone else involved or even request a full transcript.
Here’s the latest on the ‘Cornell 7’ frat probe:
- Outraged Cornell students, parents demand accountability in Jane Doe gang-rape case: ‘Fight like hell’

- The sick, online posts that pushed Cornell 7 rape accuser to go to cops: ‘I was a sex doll’
- Everything we know about explosive ‘Cornell 7’ rape case shocking the nation
“No institution gets to protect its reputation at the expense of a young person seeking justice. No public official gets to look the other way when the system breaks down and fails our young people. And as governor, I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” she declared.
Cornell University Police previously told The Post “all investigatory information” from Doe’s case had been shared with the DA’s office in 2024, but didn’t specify if that included the transcript.
The case made national headlines after the Cornell student, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit in Manhattan Supreme Court last month accusing seven fraternity brothers of raping her at the Cornell’s Phi Chi fraternity house in October 2024.
The 101-page lawsuit alleges the men plied her with alcohol and ketamine and subjecting her to an hours-long sexual assault.
While she was being assaulted, one of the men allegedly sent a message to a 50-person fraternity Snapchat group called “Chi Phi Actives,” declaring there was “free p–sy” in the house.
Doe slammed Cornell’s internal Title IX investigation process, which involved 12 hearings, and claimed her alleged attackers only got a slap on the wrist — with just two of the seven expelled from the university, the lawsuit claims.
The Ivy League school denied Doe’s claims and said the university acted in accordance with police and banned the Chi Phi frat chapter from campus.

sources.news_title: N.Y. governor says Cornell rape accuser was ‘failed’ by people obligated to protect her
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul says Jane Doe in Cornell case was ‘failed’ by the system
sources.text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday she believes the former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang raped by fraternity members in 2024 was “failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her,” including a county prosecutor.
“I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” Hochul told reporters at a Friday morning news conference in New York City.
Hochul, reading from prepared remarks, confirmed that she has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to carry out a “fresh and thorough review” of all the facts in the case nearly two years after a district attorney declined to pursue criminal charges.
“We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions,” James said at the news conference. “I know that you want answers. I do, too.”
Hochul said she believes Cornell University did not provide enough information about the accuser’s account of the alleged sexual assault at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. Hochul also faulted Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten for not doing a more comprehensive investigation.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript” of Jane Doe’s interview with Cornell University campus police, Hochul said.

“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” Hochul added.
In a statement after Hochul’s news conference, Van Houten said he supported James’ appointment, adding: “I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law.
“It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the University,” Van Houten said. “The focus has been and should continue to be on the victims. My office will cooperate fully with the Attorney General.”
Hochul said she backs proposed changes to current New York state law, which makes it difficult for a person who has voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs to seek criminal justice for an alleged sexual assault.
“Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul told reporters. “I support closing this loophole, and will work with the New York state Legislature to accomplish this.”
The accuser, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, reported the alleged assault to university police in November 2024, about three weeks after she said it took place, according to a civil lawsuit. The Ivy League university then sent a sworn statement to Van Houten’s office.
Van Houten’s office “determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime,” the district attorney has said. In a lengthy statement Monday, Van Houten said the sworn statement Jane Doe provided to campus police “did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped.”
But news reports have since complicated that characterization. CBS News New York, citing a transcript of a conversation between Jane Doe and investigators, reported Wednesday that she told campus police: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.
NBC News has not independently verified the transcript.
Jane Doe’s lawsuit names seven fraternity members as defendants. It also accuses the fraternity, her sorority and a bar she visited on the night of the alleged assault of negligence.
The national Chi Phi organization has called the sexual assault allegations at Cornell University “deeply concerning,” and the sorority said it could not comment on pending litigation. The bar denied serving alcohol to Jane Doe, who was under the legal drinking age at the time. Cornell has defended its 2024 investigation.
In response to a request for comment on Hochul’s news conference, a Cornell spokesperson said: “We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State’s rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case.”
The case has drawn extensive news coverage and wide attention on social media. Hollywood celebrities such as Oscar-nominated actor Florence Pugh and “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star Mariska Hargitay highlighted Jane Doe’s lawsuit on Instagram.
“This is a human issue, not a women’s issue,” Pugh wrote in an Instagram post Sunday. “We are all involved.”
If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

sources.news_title: Hochul says Cornell rape accuser was 'failed,' vows to uncover the truth
sources.text:
Hochul says Cornell rape accuser was 'failed,' vows to uncover the truth
NEW YORK (TNND) — New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she will push lawmakers to close what she described as a gap in the state's sexual-assault law, arguing that a person's voluntary intoxication should not be used to undermine whether they were able to consent.
“If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol,” Hochul said Friday. “Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period.”
Her remarks came as Hochul detailed her decision to appoint Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the Cornell University sexual assault case. Hochul said she lost faith in the Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten's ability to handle the matter after learning what she called “troubling details” about the initial investigation.
Hochul said the district attorney’s office closed the case in 2024 without interviewing the woman who reported the alleged attack, anyone else involved, or requesting the full transcript of her lengthy interview with Cornell police. The DA reopened the case last month after the woman, identified as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit.
The governor also criticized Cornell police over reports that its account to prosecutors did not include the woman’s statement that she was “100% confident” she had been raped.
“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” Hochul said. “And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
James said her office will “review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions.” Hochul said the attorney general will oversee the criminal investigation and could present evidence to a grand jury if warranted.
Van Houten said in a statement that he supports the appointment of James and trusts "she will examine the facts and apply the law."
"It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the University," he continued. "The focus has been and should continue to be on the victims. My office will cooperate fully with the Attorney General."
A reporter also questioned James about an earlier social-media post in which she called what the woman had been forced to endure “horrific and unacceptable” and wrote, “We stand with you.”
James declined to comment on the post, while Hochul said she had confidence the attorney general would examine the evidence and draw the proper conclusions.
